title: Prefetch, Shellbags & Application Traces
description: Discover program execution proof, folder access patterns, and artifacts left by browsers and apps.

slides.title: Prefetch: Program Execution Proof ⚡
slides.content:
# What is Prefetch?

Windows Prefetch files (`.pf`) are created to speed up application loading. They are stored in `C:\Windows\Prefetch`.

Each time an executable runs, Windows creates or updates a .pf file (up to 1024 entries on Win10). The file name is `<EXENAME>-<HASH>.pf`.

Inside the .pf file:
- **Run count** (how many times executed)
- **Last run time** (embedded within the file, not the filesystem timestamp)
- **List of loaded modules** (DLLs) for the first 10 seconds of execution

Prefetch is a strong indicator that a program was executed, even if the executable is now deleted.

quizData.question: Where are Prefetch files stored on a Windows system?

slides.title: Parsing Prefetch Files 🔧
slides.content:
Tools like **PECmd.exe** (Eric Zimmerman) extract:
- Executable name
- Run count
- Last run time(s)
- Files and directories referenced by the program during startup

This can reveal not only that a malicious executable ran, but also what files it touched (e.g., `cmd.exe` accessing a batch script).

Example: `PECmd.exe -f CMD.EXE-01234567.pf`

slides.content: Parse all Prefetch files in a folder.

quizData.question: A Prefetch file for a deleted executable can still prove the executable was run.
quizData.explanation: Prefetch files persist after the executable is deleted, retaining run count and last execution time.

slides.title: Shellbags: Folder Access Patterns 🗂️
slides.content:
Shellbags are registry keys that remember folder view settings (size, position, icon size). They are stored under:
- `HKCU\Software\Classes\Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU`
- `HKCU\Software\Classes\Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Bags`

Every time a user opens a folder in Explorer, a Shellbag entry is created/updated. Even if the folder is deleted, the Shellbag entry remains, giving a permanent record of folder browsing.

They can show:
- Access to encrypted containers (e.g., VeraCrypt volumes mounted as drives)
- Traversal of directory structures during data theft

Parse with **ShellBags Explorer** or `sbag` (TZWorks).

quizData.question: Shellbags provide evidence of ___ accessed through Windows Explorer, even if those folders no longer exist.
quizData.explanation: Shellbags track folder browsing activity, recording each folder the user opened in Explorer.

slides.title: Browser & Application Artifacts 🌐
slides.content:
While browsers store history in databases, Windows also records:
- **SRUM (System Resource Usage Monitor)**: Tracks application resource usage, network data sent/received per process, and execution time (database in `C:\Windows\System32\sru`).
- **BAM (Background Activity Moderator)** / **DAM**: Registry keys (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\State\UserSettings\...`) that record the last execution time of every executable.
- **Amcache.hve**: Records installed applications and their execution timestamps (store in `C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve`).

These additional sources provide secondary proof of program execution.

quizData.question: The BAM key in the registry records every executable that has ever been run, along with its last execution time.
quizData.explanation: BAM (Background Activity Moderator) tracks executable paths and the last execution timestamp for all users.
